analysis.one_liner: Creates a USDA watchdog to investigate big meatpackers and funds farm and ethanol fixes to cut food and fuel costs.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 221-204 on June 16, 2022, but the Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on it and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written during 2022's food and gas price spike, this bill would create a USDA office with subpoena power to investigate and sue big meatpackers over unfair and anticompetitive practices under the Packers and Stockyards Act. It also spends about $700 million to help farmers cut fertilizer costs, build new livestock and poultry processing plants, and install ethanol and biodiesel pumps, and it makes year-round sales of 15% ethanol gasoline easier. The House passed it 221-204, but the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Grocery shoppers facing high meat and gas prices, through new competition enforcement against the handful of firms that dominate meatpacking and easier year-round sales of higher ethanol blends. Ranchers and poultry growers would gain a cop against unfair dealing by the few big buyers of their animals, plus new federally backed processing options. Small and mid-size farmers would get up to $500 million in payments to cut fertilizer costs and adopt precision agriculture, and fuel retailers and terminal operators could compete for $200 million in ethanol and biodiesel infrastructure grants.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a USDA Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters that can subpoena records and bring civil or administrative actions against packers and live poultry dealers for violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act, the 1921 law governing fair dealing in livestock markets.
Provides $500 million in payments to farmers, covering up to 100% of costs, to reduce fertilizer expenses and adopt precision agriculture practices.

Creates the Butcher Block Act loans (up to $50 million, $100 million for cooperatives) and $20 million a year in grants to build and expand livestock and poultry processing, with companies processing over 5% of a species' daily harvest barred from the loans.

Appropriates $200 million in grants for fuel stations and terminals to install higher-ethanol and biodiesel dispensers and distribution systems, and extends the E10 gasoline volatility waiver to higher blends so 15% ethanol gasoline can be sold year-round.
Authorizes $100 million to address fertilizer shortages and reduce dependence on foreign fertilizer, and creates at least six regional resource centers supporting small and mid-size farm businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers and live poultry dealers, who would face a dedicated USDA office with subpoena power and authority to sue them under the Packers and Stockyards Act, and any company already processing more than 5% of a species' daily harvest, which would be barred from the new meat-processing loans. Taxpayers would fund about $700 million in emergency spending on farm payments and fuel infrastructure, plus roughly $430 million more in authorized amounts for fertilizer, processing grants, and rural centers.

drawbacks.text: The bill's emergency appropriations fund the farm payments ($500 million) and ethanol infrastructure ($200 million), but the new investigator office itself gets no dedicated money, so its enforcement power would depend entirely on future funding and the administration's willingness to use it.

The ethanol provisions mainly expand a market for an established industry: the year-round E15 waiver and $200 million in pump and terminal grants help ethanol producers and fuel retailers, with only an indirect and modest benefit to drivers.

Nothing in the bill caps meat or grocery prices; relief for shoppers depends on whether investigations and new processors actually change packer conduct, and the fertilizer payments go to producers of all sizes, including large operations, with savings reaching consumers only if they pass through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest part of the bill is the special investigator, which gives real teeth — subpoenas and independent lawsuit authority — to a Packers and Stockyards Act that has long been weakly enforced against four dominant meatpackers. But the office is unfunded in the bill, so even on paper its consumer benefit was contingent. The spending side is a familiar farm-bill mix: genuinely useful help for farmers' fertilizer bills and new processors, alongside ethanol subsidies whose consumer payoff is small. The larger issue is that none of it happened: the House passed it with a strong majority and the Senate let it die without a vote, so shoppers and ranchers got nothing while the concentrated meatpacking market stayed as it was.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a 221-204 vote, but the Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on it and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The House Agriculture Committee reported the bill as amended on a 27-21 vote on June 7, 2022.
A Republican motion to send the bill back to committee failed 206-218, with 206 of 209 Republicans in favor and all 218 voting Democrats opposed.
The House passed the bill 221-204 on June 16, 2022, with 214 of 220 Democrats voting yes and only 7 of 209 Republicans.
The Senate received the bill on June 21, 2022, and referred it to the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpackers are better off: the dedicated USDA prosecutor who could subpoena and sue them never came into being, and the bill's farm, processing, and ethanol spending never took effect. Consumers and ranchers are left with the same meat market structure they had before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big meatpackers; the enforcement threat died

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 214 of 220 House Democrats voted yes and only 7 of 209 House Republicans did; on the failed motion to recommit, 206 of 209 Republicans voted yes and 218 of 220 Democrats voted no.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers and live poultry dealers
industries.note: The bill creates a USDA Special Investigator for Competition Matters with subpoena power and authority to sue packers under the Packers and Stockyards Act, and bars any company processing over 5% of a species' daily harvest from the new processing loans. Their potential legal exposure is ranchers' and shoppers' potential gain.

The bill appropriates $200 million for grants to install higher-ethanol and biodiesel dispensers and distribution systems, and extends the E10 gasoline volatility waiver to blends above 10%, making year-round E15 sales possible. This permanently expands the market channel for ethanol with a modest fuel-price benefit to drivers.

Competition enforcement against dominant packers targets the concentrated buyer side of livestock markets, and the Butcher Block Act loans and grants would give producers more places to sell their animals.

Federally backed loans of up to $50 million ($100 million for cooperatives) and grants would finance new and expanding processing plants, explicitly excluding the biggest existing processors from eligibility.

Fueling stations, terminals, and distribution facilities are the eligible grantees for the $200 million biofuel infrastructure program, and the ethanol waiver changes their volatility compliance rules for higher blends.
The bill authorizes $100 million in grants and loans to diversify fertilizer sources, support domestic production and alternatives, and address competition problems in the fertilizer market.
